newsitem.title: BELGIUM: OLO CURVE FLATTENS, MKT NOT WORRIED ABOUT BUDGET.
newsitem.headline: OLO CURVE FLATTENS, MKT NOT WORRIED ABOUT BUDGET.

text.p: Belgian linear bonds rose in early Wednesday trade on the back of firmer Bunds, but dealers said volume remained very thin as investors waited for higher yields before investing more cash in bonds.
Dealers reported a slight flattening of the curve as institutional investors sold two to three year paper for five to seven year paper in a bid to get a higher yield pick-up.

After recommendations for continued austerity by the High Finance Council on Tuesday the focus was on the 1998 budget, to be drafted after the summer. Dealers said the market was not at all worried about the outlook for government finances.
"Nobody worries about the budget, just look at the OLO/Bund spread," one dealer said.
The spread was unchanged at eight basis points. The benchmark 2007 OLO yielded 5.76 percent, down from 5.78 Tuesday.

The High Finance Council said in its annual report that it expected Belgium's 1997 deficit to fall to 2.8 percent of GDP from a revised 3.2 percent for 1996 and below the government's 2.9 percent target.
It added the government, in cooperation with Belgium's regions, should aim to reduce the deficit further to 2.3 percent of GDP in 1998.

In its three-year budget plan, laid down in October 1996 along with the 1997 budget, the government planned to cut the deficit to 2.5 percent in 1998, 2.0 percent in 1999 and 1.6 percent in the year 2000. In a newspaper interview published on Tuesday, Budget Minister Herman Van Rompuy gave an optimistic outlook about the budget.

Front-month OLO futures were up 0.28 at 121.14 by 0835 GMT. Looking at the expiring June contract chartists said the picture was improving as the large head and shoulders formation begun in October seemed to have been broken by this month's push above 122 (the top of the right shoulder).

They noted, however, that in Bunds the head and shoulder formation was still intact, with the right shoulder level not broken on the upside. But if the market continued sideways, the formation would peter out.
The large head and shoulders had long been seen as a warning that the long-term uptrend could reverse.
